pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Subtraction as an unknown-addend problem — understanding that 10 − 8 = ? is the same question as 8 + ? = 10, so subtraction can be solved by finding the missing part / counting on. Ages 6–7, a key bridge from take-away to the additive structure.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): supports Y1–Y2 'represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts' and 'recall and use addition and subtraction facts', where subtraction facts are derived from known addition bonds; underpins missing-number problems like 7 = □ − 9.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.4 'Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem. For example, subtract 10 − 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.'
• Operational details: reframe the take-away picture as a missing-part picture on a part-whole model — whole known, one part known, find the other part. Encourage counting on from the subtrahend to the minuend, especially when the parts are close (12 − 9 by counting up 9→10→11→12). This is the efficiency insight, not just an alternative.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — given 9 + □ = 13, matches it to 13 − 9 and finds 4. Tier B (age 7) — chooses to count on for 12 − 9 because the numbers are close, and explains why. Tier C (age 7+) — states that every subtraction can be rewritten as an addition with a missing part and uses it to solve/check.
bestPractices: Anchor on the part-whole model: subtraction reveals a missing PART when the whole and one part are known.
Teach counting-up (shopkeeper's method) explicitly as the efficient strategy when subtrahend and minuend are close.
Pair each subtraction with its unknown-addend twin (13 − 9 = ? ↔ 9 + ? = 13) so the equivalence is repeatedly seen.
Use missing-number equations in varied positions to force the additive reading rather than a take-away action.
Delay pure take-away drilling; contrast 'how many are left' with 'how many more to reach' so difference/missing-part meanings are established.
keyRepresentations: Part-whole (cherry) diagram with the missing part as the unknown
Bar model: total bar with one part shaded and the gap to find
Empty number line showing a count-on jump from subtrahend to minuend
Double ten-frame with one frame filled and the gap to ten visible
Fact-family triangle linking the whole and its two parts
commonMisconceptions: Believing subtraction can only mean 'take away / count back', so refusing to count up.
Not seeing 8 + ? = 10 and 10 − 8 = ? as the same question.
Counting back inefficiently for close numbers (12−11 counted back eleven steps) and making errors.
Confusing which quantity is the whole and which is a part in the part-whole model.
Treating the answer to 8 + ? = 10 as 10 (writing the whole) rather than the missing part.

learn.summary: Help 6–7 year-olds understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem: 12 − 9 = ? asks the same question as 9 + ? = 12 — find the missing PART of a known whole. Anchor the equivalence on a part-whole model, teach counting up from the subtrahend when the numbers are close, and repeatedly pair each subtraction with its addition twin. A linked part-whole/number-line display can make the 'same gap, two routes' insight concrete; dialogue draws out the justification; matching and missing-number tasks consolidate; a static part-whole picture (with a double ten-frame and fact-family triangle as further representations) anchors both equations against one diagram.

activities.title: Two routes, one gap: linked part-whole and number line
feedback: When both routes land on the same gap, say: 'Taking away and counting up reached the same number — because they are the same question asked two ways.'
If the child gets 4 on 12 − 9 by counting back including the start (or by counting up starting on 9), replay the count-up: 9→10→11→12 is three jumps; count them together on the line.
If the child writes the whole (12) as the missing addend, point to the gap on the bar: 'We already know this part is 9; we are looking for the piece that fills the rest up to 12.'
activities.rationale: Showing the same situation two ways at once — take-away and count-on landing on one gap — can make the unknown-addend equivalence visible from a single action, and close-number cases let the child feel why counting up is often more efficient. Dragging to remove, hopping up the line, and the two equations updating together are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.4 requires understanding subtraction as an unknown-addend problem, e.g. subtract 10−8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.

Missing-addend problems are conceptually harder than take-away and children often solve subtraction by counting back even when counting up is more efficient; deriving subtraction from known addition facts is a documented strategy.
Y1–Y2 pupils represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts and solve missing-number problems, deriving subtraction facts from addition bonds.
learnerActions: Look at a part-whole bar with whole 10 and known part 8, and a number line beside it.
First try to count BACK from the whole by the known part (back 8 from 10) to find the missing part; notice this is fiddly for some pairs.
Then start at the known part (8) and hop UP to the whole (8→9→10), counting the jumps to find the gap.
See both routes highlight the SAME gap of 2, and read the two printed sentences 10 − 8 = 2 and 8 + 2 = 10 together.
Repeat with a close-number case such as 12 − 9: count back nine steps, then instead start at 9 and hop up 9→10→11→12 (three easy jumps), and see 12 − 9 = 3 printed above 9 + 3 = 12.
activities.intendedInsight: A subtraction and its unknown-addend twin ask the same question — the missing part of a whole — and counting up from the subtrahend is often the shortcut, especially when the numbers are close.

activities.title: Explain why counting up works
feedback: If the child says the two are 'different sums', put 12 as the whole and 9 as a known part on a part-whole model and show the single missing part answers BOTH questions.
Affirm reasoning that names the missing part: 'Yes — the number you add to 9 to reach 12 is the same as the number left when you take 9 from 12.'
activities.rationale: The equivalence is a reasoning insight, so inviting the child to explain why counting up works and to state the addition twin targets the conceptual 'understand as' objective. Responsive spoken discussion lets a tutor probe the justification directly; recognition-only tasks would not elicit this spoken justification.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.4 requires understanding subtraction as an unknown-addend problem, e.g. subtract 10−8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.
learnerActions: Solve a close-number subtraction such as 12 − 9 using whatever method you choose.
Answer aloud: 'You could take 9 away — but is there a quicker way to get from 9 up to 12?'
State the matching addition sentence (9 + ? = 12) for the subtraction.
Explain in your own words why 12 − 9 and 9 + ? = 12 are the same question.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify the equivalence — not just produce the number — shows the child reads subtraction additively rather than only as take-away.

activities.title: Match, fill, and choose the quicker route
feedback: For 9 + □ = 13: the missing part is 4, not 13 — 13 is the whole; underline the gap being asked for.
For the 'quicker route' choice, affirm counting up for 12 − 9 because 9 and 12 are close (three jumps) while counting back nine steps invites errors.
If the child reverses whole and part, restate: the whole is the total; the two parts add to it.
activities.rationale: Matching, missing-number and strategy-choice tasks consolidate an already-built idea. A fixed sequence of items consolidates and checks recognition and strategy choice rather than letting the child freely toggle representations, so it is best used after the linked model and paired with an explanation prompt.
sourceClaims: Y1–Y2 pupils represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts and solve missing-number problems, deriving subtraction facts from addition bonds.

Missing-addend problems are conceptually harder than take-away and children often solve subtraction by counting back even when counting up is more efficient; deriving subtraction from known addition facts is a documented strategy.
learnerActions: Match each subtraction to its unknown-addend twin, e.g. 13 − 9 ↔ 9 + □ = 13.
Fill in the missing addend: 9 + □ = 13 (answer 4), then write the matching subtraction 13 − 9 = 4.
Decide which is quicker for 12 − 9 — counting up or counting back — and give a reason.
Given a known fact such as 8 + 5 = 13, write a subtraction you can now answer straight away.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the pairing of subtraction with its addition twin and the strategic choice of counting up when numbers are close.

activities.title: One diagram, both equations (anchor)
feedback: Point at the gap: 'This is the part we are finding — it completes 8 up to 10.'
If the child names the whole as the answer, re-point to the known part and the gap.
On the ten-frame, the empty cells show the same gap (2 empty cells when 8 of 10 are filled); on the triangle, the whole sits apart from its two parts.
activities.rationale: A static part-whole picture can present both equations against one diagram and reveal the missing part, which anchors the equivalence; a double ten-frame and fact-family triangle offer the same structure in other forms. It does not let the child act out take-away and count-on as the same gap, so use it as an anchor or for learners who need a settled reference rather than as the primary builder.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.4 requires understanding subtraction as an unknown-addend problem, e.g. subtract 10−8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.
learnerActions: Look at a part-whole diagram with a tappable whole and one known part.
Tap or lift a flap to reveal the missing part.
Read both equation forms shown side by side against the same diagram, e.g. 10 − 8 = 2 and 8 + 2 = 10.
Name which number is the whole and which are the parts.

Compare the same whole and parts in other representations — a ten-frame with 8 cells filled and the gap of 2 to ten visible (use a double ten-frame for wholes above 10, e.g. 9 filled plus 3 more to reach 12), and a fact-family triangle linking the whole and its two parts — and read how each shows the missing part.
activities.intendedInsight: Both the subtraction and its addition twin describe the same part-whole picture, and the answer is the missing part.

constraints: Target ages 6–7; this bridges take-away toward the additive structure of subtraction.

The static part-whole picture and the matching/missing-number tasks consolidate or anchor; they do not let the child freely toggle between the take-away and count-on views, which the linked model provides.

Matching and multiple-choice items check recognition and strategy choice; they do not by themselves elicit the child's own spoken or written justification of why the two questions share an answer — pair them with an explanation prompt.

Teach counting up explicitly as the efficient strategy when subtrahend and minuend are close; do not present it as universally faster — for a pair like 12 − 3, counting back three is quicker, so prompt strategy choice by how near the numbers are.
Delay pure take-away drilling; contrast 'how many are left' with 'how many more to reach' so both difference and missing-part meanings are established.

Watch the count-up step count: 9→10→11→12 is three jumps; starting the count on the subtrahend itself (or counting back including the start) produces an off-by-one error (answer 4). This is a procedural slip, not a conceptual one — model the count rather than reteaching the concept.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the DfE National Curriculum claim as verified:true and the CCSS 1.OA.4 and Cognitively Guided Instruction claims as verified:false; these flags were not re-checked here.
The double ten-frame (gap-to-ten) and fact-family triangle representations from the original keyRepresentations are preserved in the anchor activity.

The recommendation narrative for 12 − 9 uses a gap of 3 (9→10→11→12), while the worked example for 10 − 8 uses a gap of 2 (8→9→10); both are arithmetically correct. Confirmed 9 + 3 = 12 and 8 + 2 = 10, and 9 + 4 = 13.

The off-by-one answer of 4 for 12 − 9 arises from miscounting the up-jumps (counting the start) or counting back including the start; handled as a strategy/counting fix, not a conceptual reteach, consistent with the source.

probeDeeper: You found 3. In this story, is 3 a part or the whole? How do you know?
What's your evidence that 9 + 3 and 12 − 9 have the same answer?
What if it were 12 − 3 instead? Would counting up still be the quick way, or would counting back be quicker — and why?
If I tell you that 8 + 5 = 13, what subtraction could you answer straight away?
assess.correctAnswer: 3 — and explains that 12 − 9 asks the same question as 9 + ? = 12: the number you add to 9 to reach 12 is the same as the number left when you take 9 from 12, so both give 3. Often solved by counting up from 9.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Subtraction just means take away, so it isn't an adding question' — gets 3 by counting back but insists 12−9 and 9+?=12 are different, unrelated sums.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach in place on a part-whole model: put 12 as the whole and 9 as a known part, and show the single missing part answers BOTH questions; do not drill more take-away.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: solves the subtraction yet cannot connect it to the addition, or calls them 'different sums'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The answer to 9 + ? = 12 is 12' — writes the whole (or adds the visible numbers) instead of the missing part.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the part-whole diagram to name which piece is the whole and which is the unknown part; point at the gap that is being asked for.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked the addition twin, says 12 (the total) rather than 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts back for close numbers and slips by one (starts the count on 9 rather than the first step), giving 4.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — model counting UP for close numbers and prompt strategy choice by how near the numbers are; check the count with fingers or a number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 4; on watching, counts '9, 10, 11, 12' as four steps or counts back including the start.

responseLevels.gap: Solves only by counting back (or not at all) and treats 12−9 and 9+?=12 as unrelated; cannot state the matching addition.
responseLevels.full: Explains that 12−9 and 9+?=12 ask the same thing (the missing part of a whole), chooses to count up when the numbers are close, and uses a known addition fact to answer a new related subtraction.
responseLevels.partial: Gets 3 and, when prompted, can state 9+3=12, but treats it as a separate fact — cannot explain why the two questions share an answer and does not transfer to a new pair.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a subtraction: 12 − 9. Work out the answer. Then tell me how this is the same as the addition 9 + ? = 12.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds only a take-away conception can still reach 3 by counting back, but stalls or denies the link on the second tier — they cannot say why 9 + ? = 12 gives the same result. A child with the unknown-addend concept answers the 'why' immediately and frequently prefers counting up because the numbers are close. The REASON tier separates the two even when both produce the numeric answer.
